evaluated.name: Externally financed asset growth
evaluated.hypothesis: Asset growth is only value-destroying when the firm cannot fund it from internal cash flow; expansion by free-cash-flow-negative (low-quality) firms reflects empire building and external capital dependence, whereas self-funded growth is disciplined.
evaluated.reasoning: The indicator switches asset growth on only for firms whose operating cash flow fails to cover capex, isolating the fragile-expansion subset from the productive-expansion subset. Internally funded growers keep a zero signal and are pooled at the neutral point, so the long-short spread is driven by financing-constrained overinvestors rather than by the unconditional asset-growth effect. Coverage stays broad because oancf, capx and at are widely reported.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Margin-validated capex expansion
evaluated.hypothesis: Capex acceleration is a positive signal when gross margins are on an improving multi-year path (evidence of profitable capacity) and a negative signal when margins are deteriorating (capacity added into a decaying business).
evaluated.reasoning: The SIGN of the five-year gross-margin trend flips the ranked capex-growth intensity, so the same investment level maps to opposite extremes depending on realized operating quality. This directly tests the productive-versus-unproductive expansion distinction rather than penalizing investment uniformly, and yields a spread between validated investors (long) and unvalidated investors (short).
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory bloat with weak profitability
evaluated.hypothesis: Working-capital investment that outruns sales growth indicates demand misjudgment; this is far more informative about future returns at low-profitability firms, which lack the margin cushion to absorb obsolete or discounted inventory.
evaluated.reasoning: The first term is an investment-quality wedge (inventory growth in excess of sales growth), and the rank of negative three-year average ROA weights it toward structurally weak firms. High-ROA firms building inventory ahead of demand are treated as near-neutral, so the spread reflects unproductive working-capital expansion instead of generic asset growth.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Intangible-led expansion with accrual-inflated earnings
evaluated.hypothesis: Expansion that arrives through purchased intangibles and goodwill rather than organic capacity is punished when reported earnings are accrual-based rather than cash-backed, because accrual-heavy acquirers are the firms most likely to be buying growth to sustain an unsustainable earnings path; cash-backed intangible expanders should not be penalized.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing raw aqc with the annual change in the intangible share of assets gives a continuous investment channel across the whole cross-section (amortization makes non-acquirers mildly negative), eliminating the acquirer/non-acquirer mass point, and its RANK acts as a smooth conditioning weight rather than an on/off switch. The industry-demeaned accrual term is signed, so high-intangible-growth firms with cash-backed earnings load on the long leg while accrual-inflated expanders load on the short leg — a genuine sign flip that the mechanical intersection of the acquirer and accrual anomalies cannot produce.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Financing-deficit-weighted capacity growth
evaluated.hypothesis: Growth in gross physical capacity destroys value when the firm's investment outlay exceeds internally generated operating cash flow, and is benign or value-creating when capacity is added out of internal cash; the same expansion therefore carries opposite information depending on internal funding capacity.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the gen-0 zero-mass failure: the binary FCF-negative switch is replaced by a continuous, industry-demeaned financing-deficit z-score, so every firm receives a signed weight and the quantile breakpoints are non-degenerate while the strong cross-sectional slope channel is preserved. Self-funded capacity builders now load on the long leg rather than piling up at exactly zero, which should convert the gen-0 FMB t-stat of -3.9 into a real long-short alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expansion beyond replacement at low cash profitability
evaluated.hypothesis: Capex far in excess of depreciation is net capacity expansion rather than maintenance; expansion is only justified when the existing asset base already generates high cash profitability, so aggressive net expansion by cash-poor firms signals overinvestment.
evaluated.reasoning: Scaling capex by depreciation separates replacement investment from genuine expansion using the firm's own capital-consumption benchmark, a distinct construction from asset or capex growth rates, and the signed industry-demeaned three-year cash-ROA multiplier flips the interpretation across quality tiers instead of merely attenuating it. Both legs are continuous and densely populated, so portfolio composition should be stable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity-funded growth without retained earnings
evaluated.hypothesis: Financing expansion with new equity is most damaging at firms with little or negative accumulated retained earnings, because such firms have no demonstrated history of internally generating profit and are effectively funding unproven growth with market capital.
evaluated.reasoning: Retained earnings scaled by assets is a stock measure of cumulative earnings quality and firm maturity, a different quality dimension from flow profitability, accruals, or volatility used elsewhere in the archive. Interacting it with equity-issuance intensity separates seasoned self-financed issuers (long leg) from cash-burning issuers (short leg), and both inputs are broadly reported so coverage should match the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth minus gross-profit growth
evaluated.hypothesis: Productive investment shows up as gross profit growing at least as fast as the physical asset base it is built on; when capacity and inventory expand faster than gross profit, the new assets are not earning, signaling low-quality expansion and future disappointment.
evaluated.reasoning: This generalizes the one gen-0 winner from inventory-versus-sales to total physical capacity versus gross profit, making the quality benchmark a margin-bearing flow rather than raw revenue, and it embeds the interaction in the wedge itself rather than as a multiplicative weight — which the critic noted only attenuates. It is a self-scaling, densely populated signal that avoids both zero-mass and rank-attenuation failure modes.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Labor bloat with margin compression
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose headcount grows faster than revenue are investing in labor capacity that is not earning, and this is most damaging when unit economics are simultaneously deteriorating; firms shedding labor while revenue and margins improve are harvesting genuine efficiency gains.
evaluated.reasoning: The multiplicative form is replaced by a wedge plus a co-ranked quality channel, so the mapping is monotone in the intended direction throughout: the high tail is hiring-faster-than-sales with falling gross margins, and the low tail is headcount discipline with margin expansion, eliminating the sign inconsistency the critic identified. Dropping the five-year sale/emp trend for one-year growth differences and a one-year margin change also removes the long-window coverage penalty while keeping labor as a distinct investment channel.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Investment-quality rank divergence
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is whether a firm's capital expansion is commensurate with its demonstrated operating quality and balance-sheet capacity: firms whose investment rank far exceeds their quality rank are over-extending, while firms whose quality exceeds their investment rank retain unexploited internal capacity.
evaluated.reasoning: Both channels are industry-ranked on the same bounded scale and enter with equal weight and opposite signs, so the signal cannot be an attenuated quality composite — its dispersion comes from the mismatch between the two themes rather than from the quality score alone. Replacing five-year earnings volatility with cash profitability and leverage keeps the quality gauge economically rich while preserving coverage, and the difference-of-ranks structure is a genuinely different design from the multiplicative and wedge families already in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Total outlay expansion with weak working-capital solvency
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), DELTA(invt, 1)), at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), lt), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Total investment outlay — physical capex plus acquisitions plus inventory build — is dangerous specifically at firms whose net working capital is thin relative to total liabilities, because they lack the balance-sheet slack to absorb a shortfall in the new assets' payoff.
evaluated.reasoning: The investment leg broadens from capex alone to the full cash outlay on growth (with unreported acquisitions correctly read as zero), while the quality leg switches from cash-flow generation to a stock measure of balance-sheet slack, a dimension absent from the archive. This tests whether the funding-fragility mechanism operates through solvency slack as well as through cash-flow coverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Investing into falling capital productivity
evaluated.hypothesis: Adding capacity while the existing asset base is generating progressively less revenue per dollar of assets signals overcapacity and demand misjudgment, whereas heavy investment accompanied by rising asset turnover reflects capacity that is already being absorbed.
evaluated.reasoning: The quality gauge is capital productivity change rather than a profitability or accrual level, so the signal is not another q-theory profitability interaction, and the denominators (ppent for investment intensity, at for turnover) avoid the mechanical small-PPE artifact that a sale/ppe pairing would create. Utilization deterioration is observable before margins deteriorate, so it may lead the profitability-based versions in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-buffer depletion during expansion
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1), MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Heavy investment financed by drawing down liquid reserves at firms that also generate weak operating cash flow is the most fragile form of expansion, since both the internal flow and the stock of internal funding are being exhausted simultaneously.
evaluated.reasoning: This separates the stock (change in cash holdings) from the flow (three-year cash ROA) dimension of internal funding and co-ranks them, rather than using the capx-minus-oancf gap, so it is not a rescaling of the archive's winner but a test of whether the liquidity buffer carries independent information. Both inputs are densely reported, so coverage should exceed the archive's funding-gap signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Five-year capital build-up without profitability payoff
evaluated.hypothesis: Investment should eventually show up in operating cash generation; firms that have accumulated a large multi-year capital build-up with no improvement in cash profitability over the same horizon have demonstrably invested unproductively, and the market is slow to write that capital down.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than re-running the one-year funding-gap winner with cosmetic changes, this switches the mechanism to realized payoff over a matched five-year horizon: the investment leg is cumulative capex intensity (a capital-vintage state, not a growth rate) and the quality leg is the trend in cash ROA over the same window, so the signal asks whether accumulated capital earned anything. The interaction is the whole content — heavy builders with improving cash profitability sit long, heavy builders with flat or falling cash profitability sit short — which is distinct from external-financing dependence.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expansion with stretched asset lives
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, LAG(ppegt, 1)), MA(RATIO(dp, LAG(ppegt, 1)), 3)), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that expand while recognizing less depreciation per dollar of beginning-of-year gross property than their own recent norm are stretching asset lives to support reported earnings, so their capital spending coincides with deteriorating accounting quality rather than genuine productivity.
evaluated.reasoning: The mechanical contamination is removed by measuring the depreciation rate against beginning-of-year gross PP&E, so assets purchased during the year do not inflate the denominator while contributing only partial-year depreciation, and by benchmarking against the firm's own three-year rate rather than the cross-section, which strips industry asset mix. What remains is policy drift in write-off intensity, interacted with capex intensity, giving a short leg of aggressive expanders with softening depreciation and a long leg of expanders who write off conservatively.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity added beyond internal funding capacity
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is how far a firm's capacity additions exceed the cash its operations actually produced: large positive gaps are externally funded expansion, while large negative values are cash-generative firms holding capacity flat or shrinking, which should be rewarded.
evaluated.reasoning: Retaining the deficit magnitude on a common asset scale fixes the quadrant problem in the SIGN version: cash-rich firms that shrink now receive the most negative (bullish) values, consistent with both the asset-growth and profitability evidence, instead of being predicted to underperform. The construct is a single dense continuous variable with no rank attenuation, no zero mass, and both themes entering symmetrically, so a strong result is direct evidence that the investment-versus-internal-cash gap, not either level alone, is the priced quantity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Co-ranked outlay and solvency slack
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), DELTA(invt, 1)), at), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Heavy total investment outlay combined with thin working-capital slack relative to liabilities identifies fragile expansion, and this relation should be monotone across the cross-section rather than confined to the extreme tails.
evaluated.reasoning: The multiplicative version delivered a −4.0 t-stat alpha but a null Fama-MacBeth slope, the signature of a product whose raw scale is dominated by a few extreme observations; replacing MUL with a bounded co-rank keeps the same two economic legs while making the signal monotone and outlier-insensitive, which should convert the portfolio spread into cross-sectional slope evidence as well. This isolates operator structure only, so the comparison is directly attributable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex intensity with weak debt-service capacity
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital spending is dangerous when cash earnings cover only a small fraction of outstanding debt, because the firm must keep servicing fixed claims while the new assets are still unproductive, forcing asset sales or dilution exactly when the investment fails to pay off.
evaluated.reasoning: Debt-service capacity (funds from operations over total debt) is a distinct fragility dimension from the flow funding gap, the cash buffer, or working-capital slack already tested, and it directly captures the claim-priority mechanism behind low-quality expansion. Funds from operations and debt balances are densely reported, so coverage should be at the higher end of the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex into a multi-year gross-profitability decline
evaluated.hypothesis: Adding capacity while gross profitability on the asset base has been declining for several years signals structural erosion of the business rather than a temporary dip, and such investment should be punished more than investment during a one-year turnover wobble.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's capital-productivity signal produced a solid FMB slope but almost no alpha, consistent with a noisy one-year change in asset turnover producing unstable portfolio extremes; replacing it with a five-year trend in gross profit over assets smooths the quality leg and shifts the concept from utilization wobble to structural erosion. This isolates the smoothing/horizon choice while keeping the same capital-productivity mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Maturity-mismatched capital spending
evaluated.hypothesis: Long-lived physical investment financed against a liability structure concentrated in current obligations creates rollover risk during the gestation period before the assets produce cash, so heavy capex at firms whose liabilities are predominantly short-term should predict low returns even when the funding level looks adequate.
evaluated.reasoning: The quality dimension is liability *duration* rather than the level of internal funds, solvency slack, or cash buffer already tested, so this is new economic content: it says the mismatch between asset life and claim maturity — not the size of the funding gap — is what makes expansion fragile. The signed industry-standardized short-maturity share reorders capex intensity so that heavy investors funded with long-duration claims sit long, giving a genuine conditional interaction rather than an averaging of archive legs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Escalating capex despite poor marginal payoff
evaluated.hypothesis: The realized cash payoff on last year's capital spending is the market's best evidence on whether a firm's investment is productive; firms that keep spending heavily after their prior capital delivered little or no incremental operating cash flow are escalating commitment to failing projects.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces an average-profitability or uncertainty gauge with a *marginal* return-on-new-capital measure — the change in operating cash flow per dollar of prior-year capex — which is a mechanism no archive signal and no standard investment anomaly captures. The interaction is essential: a low marginal payoff is only bearish for firms that are still spending, while high marginal payoff plus heavy spending identifies genuinely productive investment on the long side.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Aging capital base with weak cash generation
evaluated.hypothesis: A heavily depreciated capital stock means the productive base is old and due for replacement; firms in that state with weak cash generation cannot fund renewal and face obsolescence, whereas cash-rich firms with old assets can harvest or reinvest at will.
evaluated.reasoning: Capital vintage — accumulated depreciation as a share of gross property — is an investment-theme state variable measuring past *under*-investment, the opposite pole from every expansion measure in the archive, so this tests whether the theme interaction is symmetric or specific to overexpansion. Pairing it with three-year cash ROA distinguishes obsolescence traps (short leg) from mature cash-generative harvesters (long leg), and both inputs are densely reported.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expansion financed through losses
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ib, at), ABS(RATIO(ib, at))), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Quality matters asymmetrically for investment: variation in profitability among already-profitable firms says little about whether capex is productive, but the depth of current losses says a great deal, because loss-making expanders must fund both operations and growth from outside capital.
evaluated.reasoning: The term ib/at minus its absolute value equals twice the loss magnitude and is exactly zero for every profitable firm, so the quality leg conditions only within the loss region instead of spreading weight across the whole profitability distribution — an asymmetric conditioning design the archive has never tested. The short leg is deep-loss heavy investors, the long leg is profitable heavy investors, which is precisely the productive-versus-fragile expansion contrast the theme asks for.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth with chronic deficit years
evaluated.hypothesis: What distinguishes structurally external-finance-dependent expanders from firms in a lumpy capex year is the *number* of past years in which investment exceeded operating cash flow; capacity growth by firms with a persistent deficit history should be the most value-destroying.
evaluated.reasoning: Counting deficit years over five years converts the funding-gap concept from a heavy-tailed magnitude into a bounded 0–5 state variable, so it cannot be dominated by outliers and it measures persistence rather than the current-year level — a different economic claim (chronic dependence) from the archive's one-year gap. If it beats the one-year winner on the FMB slope while holding the alpha, it identifies persistence as the operative fragility mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex with near-term refinancing pressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dlc, ADD(ib, dp)), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms committing cash to long-lived assets while their debt maturing within the year exceeds a full year of cash earnings face rollover risk exactly during the project gestation period, forcing distressed refinancing, asset sales, or dilution.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the failed maturity-mismatch signal, whose lct/lt leg inadvertently proxied for *low* leverage (giving the wrong sign); the replacement measures near-term debt net of annual funds from operations on a common asset scale, so loss-making firms with maturing debt score most fragile instead of being mis-ranked by a negative denominator. It is distinct from the FFO-to-total-debt signal because it isolates *timing* of claims rather than total leverage capacity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory bloat with signed cash profitability
evaluated.hypothesis: Working-capital investment outrunning sales is bearish at cash-poor firms and largely innocuous at cash-generative firms, which can carry and eventually clear the inventory; the quality leg should therefore reorder the wedge rather than merely shrink it.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-0 inventory-bloat winner used a non-negative ROA rank that could only attenuate, which the critic identified as its central weakness; replacing it with a signed, industry-standardized three-year cash-ROA and ranking the wedge itself makes high-bloat cash-poor firms the short leg and high-bloat cash-rich firms the long leg. This is an attributable single-element upgrade of an established archive winner along the dimension the critic flagged.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expansion on receivable-inflated revenue
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(SUB(act, invt), che), 1), GROWTH(sale, 1)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital spending justified by revenue that is being generated through looser credit terms rather than cash sales is built on a demand signal that will not persist; firms expanding capacity while receivables grow faster than sales are extrapolating low-quality revenue.
evaluated.reasoning: The quality dimension here is *revenue* quality — the receivable-versus-sales growth wedge, using non-cash non-inventory current assets — which is economically distinct from every quality leg tested so far (cash-flow funding gap, solvency slack, profitability level, accruals, leverage) and is the channel through which managers most often misread demand before committing capital. It abandons the over-explored solvency-slack interaction entirely while keeping the multiplicative conditioning structure that has generated the archive's alphas, and all inputs are densely reported one-year flows.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Investing while earnings fail to cover capital consumption
evaluated.hypothesis: Depreciation is the economic cost of the capital already in place, so a firm whose earnings fall short of its own depreciation charge has not shown that its existing assets earn their keep; committing further capital in that state is expansion financed by capital consumption rather than by profit.
evaluated.reasoning: The quality benchmark is the firm's own capital-consumption hurdle (dp versus ib on a common asset scale), which is a different economic test from cash-flow shortfall, liquidity slack, or debt coverage: it asks whether the installed capital base clears its depreciation cost before more is added. The measure is well-behaved for loss-making and low-leverage firms alike — no small or sign-flipping denominators — and it reorders capex intensity so that heavy investors earning well above depreciation sit long while capital-consuming expanders sit short.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth on receivable-inflated revenue
evaluated.hypothesis: Building capacity in response to revenue growth that is being manufactured through looser customer credit rather than cash sales is expansion premised on a demand signal that will reverse.
evaluated.reasoning: The revenue-quality wedge (receivables growing faster than sales) delivered the strongest FMB slope of the gen-4 batch (−2.97) but only −0.9% alpha when attached to capex intensity; pairing it with capacity growth tests the same investment-leg diagnosis on an entirely different quality channel, so the two swaps jointly identify whether the carrier or the channel governs portfolio performance. Both legs are one-year flows, keeping coverage near the archive's high end.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity and inventory expansion with thin solvency slack
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms growing their physical and working-capital asset base while holding little net working capital against total liabilities are expanding without the balance-sheet slack to survive a shortfall in the new assets' payoff.
evaluated.reasoning: The solvency-slack channel generated the archive's largest alphas (t = −4.05 and −4.65) but essentially no cross-sectional slope, and both prior attempts used an *outlay level* investment leg; replacing that level with the growth rate of the combined physical and inventory base changes the carrier to the type that has consistently produced monotone cross-sectional slopes, which is the one edit that could deliver both metrics at once. It also removes the mild mechanical overlap the critic noted, since Δinvt no longer appears inside the numerator of a level ratio.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Stale acquisition capital without cash-flow payoff
evaluated.hypothesis: Goodwill is capitalized evidence of past acquisitive investment whose value depends entirely on subsequent cash-flow improvement; firms carrying large goodwill balances with no multi-year improvement in cash profitability hold overstated assets and face impairment, while goodwill-heavy firms with rising cash flow have validated their acquisitions.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new mechanism — the *stock* of unproven inorganic capital judged against its realized payoff — rather than another flow-versus-funding interaction, and it targets a specific accounting event (impairment) that the market appears to anticipate slowly. Treating unreported goodwill as zero is the economically correct convention for a firm that has not made acquisitions, so coverage stays broad while the interaction remains concentrated among acquirers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth co-ranked with loss depth
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragile expansion is the joint occurrence of growing productive capacity and running losses; both features should push the signal in the same bearish direction, so that shrinking profitable firms occupy the long leg and expanding loss-makers the short leg.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly showed that z-scoring then negating the hinge gave profitable firms a common negative multiplier, making the long leg high-growth profitable firms — a bet against the asset-growth effect that the hypothesis never intended. Co-ranking instead keeps the loss channel non-negative (|x|−x equals twice the loss magnitude, zero for profitable firms) and lets capacity growth enter monotonically bearish on its own, so no quadrant contradicts either the investment or the quality evidence while the interaction still concentrates the short leg on expanding loss-makers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex surge funded by stretching trade obligations
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(capx, at), MA(RATIO(capx, at), 5)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lct, cogs), 1), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A discretionary capex surge above the firm's own norm is benign if paid for out of operations, but bearish when the firm simultaneously stretches its current obligations relative to its cost base — that is, when suppliers and other short-term claimants are effectively financing the expansion.
evaluated.reasoning: The carrier stays the within-firm capex deviation, which is what escapes the level-characteristic problem, but the quality leg is replaced with a channel the archive has never used: growth in current liabilities relative to cost of goods sold, a payables-stretching measure of low-quality operating finance. That makes the signal a test of *how the surge was funded* rather than a rediscovery of abnormal capital investment interacted with the recycled three-year cash-ROA leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Multi-channel expansion breadth with internal funding gap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(ADD(ADD(INDICATOR(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), 0), INDICATOR(GROWTH(invt, 1), 0)), INDICATOR(RATIO(COALESCE(aqc, 0), at), 0))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms expanding on every front at once — physical capacity, inventory, and acquisitions simultaneously — are in an empire-building mode that is far more dangerous when internal cash does not cover the investment programme than any single expansion channel is on its own.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than tweaking the winner's deficit numerator, this changes the carrier's structure entirely: breadth is a 0–3 count of simultaneously expanding investment channels, a diversification-of-growth-modes concept that no archive signal captures and that cannot be reproduced by any single growth rate. Pairing the new carrier with the unmodified, proven funding-gap quality leg keeps the comparison to the archive's best signal clean and attributable to the breadth construction alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Profitable expanders with an internal funding gap
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 1))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The overinvestment penalty applies to viable firms that expand beyond their internal cash generation; deep-loss expanders are a separate distress population whose returns are driven by option-like recovery risk, so weighting the funding-gap interaction toward profitable firms should sharpen the abnormal-return spread.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-5 loss-depth result showed that the deep-loss expansion tail earns strongly *positive* FF5 alpha, which means any signal that pushes loss-makers into the short leg is fighting a distress premium; multiplying the archive's best interaction by a non-negative profitability rank smoothly pulls loss-makers toward the middle without creating a zero mass. The long leg becomes profitable, self-funded expanders and the short leg profitable but externally dependent expanders — precisely the productive-versus-unproductive contrast, purged of distress.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth with flow and stock funding fragility
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragile expansion has two complementary funding dimensions — a flow shortfall (investment exceeding operating cash flow) and a stock shortfall (little working-capital slack against liabilities) — and firms failing both are the most exposed when new capacity disappoints.
evaluated.reasoning: These are the only two quality channels in the archive that have produced FF5 alphas beyond 3% annualized, and their weaknesses are complementary: the flow gap delivers the cross-sectional slope, the stock slack delivers the largest alphas but no slope. Co-ranking them inside the quality leg (bounded, so neither dominates through outliers) while holding the growth carrier fixed is a single attributable change aimed at getting slope and alpha from one construct.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth funded by outside equity
evaluated.hypothesis: The portion of a firm's book-equity increase not explained by its own earnings is external equity finance net of distributions; capacity growth paid for with outside equity rather than retained profit signals expansion the market must fund rather than expansion the business has earned.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the failed gross-issuance measure (sstk, which is contaminated by option exercises and produced almost no alpha) with a clean net measure — the change in book equity less current earnings — which nets dividends and buybacks and is defined for essentially every firm. It tests a funding *source* channel distinct from cash-flow shortfall, since a firm can have a small operating gap yet still be systematically diluting shareholders to grow.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Post-expansion profitability disappointment
evaluated.hypothesis: The market learns slowly whether last year's capacity expansion was productive; firms that expanded and then delivered falling profitability are revealed low-quality investors, and the correction continues after the disappointing report.
evaluated.reasoning: This is an event-time rather than contemporaneous interaction: the investment decision is dated one year earlier and the quality leg is the subsequent change in return on assets, so the signal captures realized failure of investment rather than the ex ante conditions surrounding it — a mechanism no archive signal has tested. It also yields a coherent long leg of prior expanders whose profitability actually improved, i.e. validated investment.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth with lengthening cash cycle
evaluated.hypothesis: Adding physical capacity at the same time that each dollar of sales requires more net working capital means the expansion is absorbing cash on two fronts and the operating cycle is deteriorating, indicating demand that must be bought with credit and inventory rather than demand that pulls product through.
evaluated.reasoning: The quality leg is the change in net working capital per dollar of sales — an operating-cycle efficiency flow that shares no term with operating cash flow, so it is not a re-labelling of the funding-gap leg and is not the Sloan accrual measure. It pairs the cash-absorption dimension of expansion with the capacity-growth carrier that has produced the archive's largest alphas, and both legs are densely reported annual flows.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth against the binding funding constraint
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), lt))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Financial fragility is set by a firm's weakest funding dimension rather than by an average of its dimensions: a firm with ample cash flow but no balance-sheet slack, or ample slack but a large cash shortfall, is exposed either way, so expansion should be punished according to the binding constraint.
evaluated.reasoning: Taking the minimum of the two ranked funding channels is a conjunctive, weakest-link aggregation that no archive signal uses, and it is a substantively different economic claim from the co-ranked average version — one says fragility compounds, the other says the binding constraint governs — so the pair jointly identifies how fragility aggregates rather than re-testing additive versus multiplicative structure. Ranking each channel before the MIN keeps the two dimensions on a common scale so neither can dominate through units or outliers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth with weak internal coverage of capex
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is what fraction of the investment programme operations actually pay for; a firm spending twice its operating cash flow is externally dependent regardless of how large that gap looks relative to total assets.
evaluated.reasoning: Normalizing internal cash by the investment programme rather than by the asset base removes the capital-intensity and size contamination in the (capx − oancf)/at scaling, and ranking the coverage ratio before standardizing handles the sign and scale pathologies that arise when operating cash flow is negative. This is a different economic normalization of the winning channel, not a rescaling of the same variable, so a comparison directly tests which funding metric the market prices.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth into decelerating demand
evaluated.hypothesis: Capacity commitments are made on extrapolated demand; firms that add capacity just as their revenue growth decelerates have misjudged the cycle and will operate the new assets below plan, whereas firms adding capacity into accelerating demand are responding to genuine absorption.
evaluated.reasoning: The quality gauge is the *acceleration* of the revenue base — a demand-momentum concept the archive has never tested, distinct from margin levels, trends, cash flow, or receivables quality — and it captures the timing error that turns investment unproductive. Both legs are dense one-year quantities, so coverage should be well above the leading signal's 0.076.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Multi-year net capital formation against funding shortfall
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(capx, dp), 3), LAG(at, 1)), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Genuine expansion is capital spending in excess of capital consumption sustained over several years; firms that have been adding net capital for three years while still failing to fund investment internally are the clearest cases of persistent, externally financed overexpansion.
evaluated.reasoning: The carrier becomes cumulative *net* capital formation (capex less depreciation over three years, asset-scaled), which strips replacement investment and single-year lumpiness from the expansion measure — a different investment state variable than either a one-year growth rate or a gross cumulative capex total. Holding the funding-gap leg unchanged keeps the comparison to the leading signal clean and tests whether persistence of net capital formation, rather than the current year's expansion, is the operative investment condition.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hiring commitments against internal funding shortfall
evaluated.hypothesis: Headcount growth is the least reversible investment a firm makes — wages must be paid every period and layoffs are costly — so hiring while investment already exceeds internal cash generation commits the firm to a fixed cash burden it cannot fund, whereas cash-generative firms can carry new staff through a slow patch.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the coverage patch with a substantively different investment channel: the carrier is an off-balance-sheet, irreversible labor commitment rather than capitalized property, which tests whether the funding-fragility mechanism is about capital formation specifically or about committing to any fixed obligation without internal funds. Employment is reported far more broadly and uniformly than gross PP&E, so tradable breadth improves for an economic reason rather than through a missing-data substitution.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expanding at peak own-history profitability
evaluated.hypothesis: Managers extrapolate temporarily good results: capacity added when profitability stands at the top of the firm's own five-year range is capacity built on a cyclical peak that will mean-revert, whereas expansion undertaken when profitability is at the low end of its own history reflects deliberate counter-cyclical investment.
evaluated.reasoning: This reverses the usual conditioning logic — it is not low profitability but *transitorily high* profitability that makes expansion unproductive — and it may explain why cross-sectional profitability levels produced slopes without alpha in this archive, since a high level relative to peers is not the same as a high level relative to the firm's own norm. TS_RANK is bounded and firm-normalized, so it introduces no outlier or industry-mix contamination into the interaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth during an inventory glut
evaluated.hypothesis: Inventory sitting at a multi-year high relative to sales means the firm cannot clear what it already produces; adding productive capacity in that state compounds an existing glut, while expanding when stock is lean relative to sales indicates demand genuinely pulling product through.
evaluated.reasoning: The quality gauge is the firm's own inventory-to-sales *position in its five-year history* — a demand-absorption state rather than the one-year inventory-versus-sales growth wedge or a margin change, so it is not a repackaging of the margin-deterioration channel the critic identified. It is bounded, firm-normalized, and densely available, and it pairs a working-capital state with the physical-capacity carrier that has produced the archive's largest alphas.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth with funding gap and inventory glut
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Expansion is worst when the firm can neither fund it internally nor sell what it already produces; the cash-shortfall and demand-absorption conditions are economically distinct and should reinforce each other.
evaluated.reasoning: The glut conditioner produced the archive's strongest Fama-MacBeth slope (−4.39) with a weak alpha, while the funding gap produces the strongest alphas with a moderate slope, so their weaknesses are complementary in exactly the way the flow-plus-stock merge was — and that merge held its alpha at −4.1% with t −3.46. Both channels are bounded before co-ranking (the glut term is a firm-normalized five-year position, the gap winsorized), so neither can dominate through outliers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory investment against the funding gap
evaluated.hypothesis: Working-capital investment is a resource commitment like capital and labor; building stock while investment already exceeds operating cash flow means the firm is financing unsold goods with outside money.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the third and final distinct commitment channel — after fixed capital and labor — and tests whether the funding-fragility mechanism is general to all resource commitments or specific to long-lived assets, which is the key question for interpreting the whole archive. Inventory change scaled by lagged assets is dense and free of the small-denominator problem in growth-rate carriers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth with a shrinking equity cushion
evaluated.hypothesis: A falling book-equity share of assets during expansion means the new capital was financed by claims senior to shareholders; the equity cushion thins exactly as operating risk rises, which is the balance-sheet counterpart of a cash-flow shortfall.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests the same fragility idea through the capital-structure channel rather than the cash-flow statement, and because it needs neither oancf nor multi-year windows it should trade on materially more firm-months than the 0.076 coverage of the leading construct. If it delivers a comparable alpha, it provides a denser, more implementable version of the mechanism; if not, it isolates internal cash generation — not leverage — as the operative condition.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Out-of-character expansion against the funding gap
evaluated.hypothesis: What signals over-extrapolation is not being a high-investment firm but making an unusually large commitment relative to the firm's own recent behaviour; a capacity jump to the top of a firm's own five-year expansion range, undertaken without internal cash, is a discretionary bet rather than a steady capital programme.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the averaging of two known parents with a genuine economic distinction the archive has never separated — cross-sectionally high expansion (partly an industry characteristic) versus expansion that is unusual for the firm — using the firm's own history to define the commitment. Habitual capital-intensive firms are pushed toward the middle regardless of their level of capex, so the extreme portfolios consist of firms changing behaviour, which is where extrapolation errors should concentrate.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth despite weak revenue payoff on prior capital
evaluated.hypothesis: The revenue generated per dollar of last year's capital spending is direct evidence on whether a firm's projects work; continuing to expand after prior capital produced little incremental revenue identifies managers escalating commitment rather than responding to demand.
evaluated.reasoning: The marginal-payoff idea previously scored only −2.4% alpha with t −1.75, but it was measured in cash flow and attached to the capex-*level* carrier that the archive has repeatedly shown cannot generate alpha; here the payoff is the incremental revenue product of prior capital and the carrier is capacity growth, which has produced every large alpha in the archive. Unlike smoothing the funding gap, this changes the economic content of the quality leg from financing capacity to realized project performance.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Non-redeployable asset expansion with thin liquid slack
evaluated.hypothesis: Assets that cannot easily be resold — installed plant and purchased intangibles — leave a firm with no exit if the investment disappoints; committing to them while holding little net working capital against total liabilities means any shortfall must be met by a fire sale of exactly the assets that have no market.
evaluated.reasoning: The carrier is an asset-redeployability concept rather than a generic growth rate: it isolates the specific, illiquid share of new investment (net plant plus intangibles, treating non-reporters of intangibles as zero) rather than total asset growth, which the critic rightly noted is a published benchmark. Pairing it with the solvency-slack channel — the one quality leg that has repeatedly delivered FF5 alphas beyond 3% — targets the fire-sale mechanism directly, and both legs avoid oancf so coverage should sit near the archive's high end.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory building into an existing overhang
evaluated.hypothesis: Adding stock when inventory relative to sales already stands at the top of the firm's own five-year range is unambiguous evidence of unsold production, whereas building stock from a lean base reflects demand the firm expects to fill.
evaluated.reasoning: This pairs the working-capital commitment channel with the demand-absorption state that matches it economically, rather than borrowing the physical-capacity carrier as the earlier glut test did, so the interaction is internally coherent: both legs describe inventory. Its inputs are dense and it needs neither cash-flow statement nor five-year capital history, so it complements the funding-gap family with an independent, high-coverage mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth with confirmed uses and sources shortfall
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), ib)), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is genuinely externally dependent only when both sides of its funding identity agree — investment exceeds internal cash *and* the firm actually went to capital markets to close the difference — so requiring both should purge measurement noise from either leg alone.
evaluated.reasoning: The uses-side gap has produced the archive's best alpha and the sources-side issuance measure its second-best slope, and unlike previous merges (gap with solvency slack, gap with inventory glut) these two legs measure the *same* economic event through independent accounting channels, so co-ranking them is a noise-reduction argument rather than an aggregation of different risks. If the combination lifts the alpha t-statistic above the leader's −3.95, it would be the strongest construct discovered in this search.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hiring commitments with thin solvency slack
evaluated.hypothesis: Payroll is a recurring cash obligation that cannot be deferred; adding headcount while holding little net working capital against total liabilities commits the firm to a fixed drain it may be unable to meet, independent of how its capital spending is financed.
evaluated.reasoning: The labor carrier has been validated only against the cash-flow funding gap (alpha −3.8%, t −3.16); pairing it with the dense solvency-slack state tests whether the two proven components combine off the cash-flow statement, which would confirm that the mechanism is about commitment versus balance-sheet capacity in general rather than about capex financing specifically. Both legs are widely reported, so coverage should be near the archive's high end rather than the leader's thin 0.076.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity growth with weak debt-service capacity
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose annual cash earnings cover only a small fraction of its outstanding debt has no capacity to absorb a disappointing project; expanding capacity from that position means the fixed claims must be serviced throughout the gestation of assets that may never earn.
evaluated.reasoning: Debt-service capacity is a *stock* leverage-capacity condition, economically distinct from the flow funding gap and from the net-external-financing quantity the critic identified as published, and it is the one quality channel in the archive that produced a genuine alpha (−2.2%, t −2.41) while attached to the capex-*level* carrier that the archive has repeatedly shown suppresses alpha. Re-pairing it with the validated capacity-growth carrier is the single highest-prior untested combination remaining, and its inputs support coverage near 0.118 rather than the leader's 0.076.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expanding at an own-history liquidity trough
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms judge their own liquidity against their own norms; committing to new capacity when cash relative to current obligations sits at the bottom of the firm's five-year range means the expansion is being undertaken with no reserve, whereas expanding from a historically strong cash position is a deliberate deployment of accumulated slack.
evaluated.reasoning: This introduces a fourth, firm-normalized conditioner — the position of cash coverage of current liabilities within the firm's own history — rather than recombining the funding gap, solvency slack, and inventory glut, and it is immune to the cross-sectional industry differences in cash policy that contaminate level-based liquidity measures. It requires no cash-flow statement and no long capital history, so it tests whether the fragility mechanism survives on a dense, purely balance-sheet state variable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Persistent net expansion without internal funding
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, dp), at), 0), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 0)), 3)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(capx, oancf), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Undisciplined capital allocation is a repeated pattern: adding capital beyond replacement needs while failing to fund it internally, in year after year, identifies management behaviour rather than a single lumpy project.
evaluated.reasoning: The degeneracy the critic identified is removed by replacing the near-always-true "gross PP&E rose" test with "capex exceeded depreciation," a genuinely binding condition satisfied by roughly half of firm-years, so the three-year count now measures the joint state rather than collapsing to a deficit count. Severity is retained through the current-year gap magnitude, giving a construct that separates chronic over-expanders from firms whose shortfall is a one-off, which the archive's earlier persistence tests could not do.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Externally financed asset growth
considered.hypothesis: Asset growth is only value-destroying when the firm cannot fund it from internal cash flow; expansion by free-cash-flow-negative (low-quality) firms reflects empire building and external capital dependence, whereas self-funded growth is disciplined.
considered.reasoning: The indicator switches asset growth on only for firms whose operating cash flow fails to cover capex, isolating the fragile-expansion subset from the productive-expansion subset. Internally funded growers keep a zero signal and are pooled at the neutral point, so the long-short spread is driven by financing-constrained overinvestors rather than by the unconditional asset-growth effect. Coverage stays broad because oancf, capx and at are widely reported.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt-funded growth without cash coverage
considered.hypothesis: New debt issuance used to expand the asset base is benign when operating cash flow comfortably services total liabilities, but predicts low returns when cash coverage is thin, since leverage-financed growth at weakly covered firms raises distress and overinvestment risk simultaneously.
considered.reasoning: The first term is asset-scaled net debt growth (an investment-financing flow), the second is a rank of inverse cash-flow coverage of liabilities (a balance-sheet quality gauge). Their product concentrates the short leg on levered expanders with poor debt-service capacity, a mechanism the standard asset-growth factor does not separate.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Margin-validated capex expansion
considered.hypothesis: Capex acceleration is a positive signal when gross margins are on an improving multi-year path (evidence of profitable capacity) and a negative signal when margins are deteriorating (capacity added into a decaying business).
considered.reasoning: The SIGN of the five-year gross-margin trend flips the ranked capex-growth intensity, so the same investment level maps to opposite extremes depending on realized operating quality. This directly tests the productive-versus-unproductive expansion distinction rather than penalizing investment uniformly, and yields a spread between validated investors (long) and unvalidated investors (short).
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Inventory bloat with weak profitability
considered.hypothesis: Working-capital investment that outruns sales growth indicates demand misjudgment; this is far more informative about future returns at low-profitability firms, which lack the margin cushion to absorb obsolete or discounted inventory.
considered.reasoning: The first term is an investment-quality wedge (inventory growth in excess of sales growth), and the rank of negative three-year average ROA weights it toward structurally weak firms. High-ROA firms building inventory ahead of demand are treated as near-neutral, so the spread reflects unproductive working-capital expansion instead of generic asset growth.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Growth with deteriorating productivity and unstable earnings
considered.hypothesis: Asset growth is value-destroying when the existing asset base is showing falling revenue productivity and unstable profitability, but value-creating when the firm is simultaneously raising asset turnover with steady earnings; the same balance-sheet expansion therefore carries opposite information depending on operating quality.
considered.reasoning: The multiplier is a within-industry standardized quality score (turnover trend net of earnings instability) that is centered at zero, so it flips rather than merely attenuates the sign of asset growth; this makes the signal close to orthogonal to plain GROWTH(at,1) instead of a monotone reweighting of it. Combining a first-moment productivity trend with a second-moment stability term also moves the quality channel beyond a pure investment-times-uncertainty construct, and both inputs come from widely reported items so coverage remains high.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Intangible-led expansion with accrual-inflated earnings
considered.hypothesis: Expansion that arrives through purchased intangibles and goodwill rather than organic capacity is punished when reported earnings are accrual-based rather than cash-backed, because accrual-heavy acquirers are the firms most likely to be buying growth to sustain an unsustainable earnings path; cash-backed intangible expanders should not be penalized.
considered.reasoning: Replacing raw aqc with the annual change in the intangible share of assets gives a continuous investment channel across the whole cross-section (amortization makes non-acquirers mildly negative), eliminating the acquirer/non-acquirer mass point, and its RANK acts as a smooth conditioning weight rather than an on/off switch. The industry-demeaned accrual term is signed, so high-intangible-growth firms with cash-backed earnings load on the long leg while accrual-inflated expanders load on the short leg — a genuine sign flip that the mechanical intersection of the acquirer and accrual anomalies cannot produce.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Financing-deficit-weighted capacity growth
considered.hypothesis: Growth in gross physical capacity destroys value when the firm's investment outlay exceeds internally generated operating cash flow, and is benign or value-creating when capacity is added out of internal cash; the same expansion therefore carries opposite information depending on internal funding capacity.
considered.reasoning: This repairs the gen-0 zero-mass failure: the binary FCF-negative switch is replaced by a continuous, industry-demeaned financing-deficit z-score, so every firm receives a signed weight and the quantile breakpoints are non-degenerate while the strong cross-sectional slope channel is preserved. Self-funded capacity builders now load on the long leg rather than piling up at exactly zero, which should convert the gen-0 FMB t-stat of -3.9 into a real long-short alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Expansion beyond replacement at low cash profitability
considered.hypothesis: Capex far in excess of depreciation is net capacity expansion rather than maintenance; expansion is only justified when the existing asset base already generates high cash profitability, so aggressive net expansion by cash-poor firms signals overinvestment.
considered.reasoning: Scaling capex by depreciation separates replacement investment from genuine expansion using the firm's own capital-consumption benchmark, a distinct construction from asset or capex growth rates, and the signed industry-demeaned three-year cash-ROA multiplier flips the interpretation across quality tiers instead of merely attenuating it. Both legs are continuous and densely populated, so portfolio composition should be stable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity-funded growth without retained earnings
considered.hypothesis: Financing expansion with new equity is most damaging at firms with little or negative accumulated retained earnings, because such firms have no demonstrated history of internally generating profit and are effectively funding unproven growth with market capital.
considered.reasoning: Retained earnings scaled by assets is a stock measure of cumulative earnings quality and firm maturity, a different quality dimension from flow profitability, accruals, or volatility used elsewhere in the archive. Interacting it with equity-issuance intensity separates seasoned self-financed issuers (long leg) from cash-burning issuers (short leg), and both inputs are broadly reported so coverage should match the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity growth minus gross-profit growth
considered.hypothesis: Productive investment shows up as gross profit growing at least as fast as the physical asset base it is built on; when capacity and inventory expand faster than gross profit, the new assets are not earning, signaling low-quality expansion and future disappointment.
considered.reasoning: This generalizes the one gen-0 winner from inventory-versus-sales to total physical capacity versus gross profit, making the quality benchmark a margin-bearing flow rather than raw revenue, and it embeds the interaction in the wedge itself rather than as a multiplicative weight — which the critic noted only attenuates. It is a self-scaling, densely populated signal that avoids both zero-mass and rank-attenuation failure modes.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Labor bloat with margin compression
considered.hypothesis: Firms whose headcount grows faster than revenue are investing in labor capacity that is not earning, and this is most damaging when unit economics are simultaneously deteriorating; firms shedding labor while revenue and margins improve are harvesting genuine efficiency gains.
considered.reasoning: The multiplicative form is replaced by a wedge plus a co-ranked quality channel, so the mapping is monotone in the intended direction throughout: the high tail is hiring-faster-than-sales with falling gross margins, and the low tail is headcount discipline with margin expansion, eliminating the sign inconsistency the critic identified. Dropping the five-year sale/emp trend for one-year growth differences and a one-year margin change also removes the long-window coverage penalty while keeping labor as a distinct investment channel.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Investment-quality rank divergence
considered.hypothesis: What matters is whether a firm's capital expansion is commensurate with its demonstrated operating quality and balance-sheet capacity: firms whose investment rank far exceeds their quality rank are over-extending, while firms whose quality exceeds their investment rank retain unexploited internal capacity.
considered.reasoning: Both channels are industry-ranked on the same bounded scale and enter with equal weight and opposite signs, so the signal cannot be an attenuated quality composite — its dispersion comes from the mismatch between the two themes rather than from the quality score alone. Replacing five-year earnings volatility with cash profitability and leverage keeps the quality gauge economically rich while preserving coverage, and the difference-of-ranks structure is a genuinely different design from the multiplicative and wedge families already in the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Total outlay expansion with weak working-capital solvency
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), DELTA(invt, 1)), at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), lt), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Total investment outlay — physical capex plus acquisitions plus inventory build — is dangerous specifically at firms whose net working capital is thin relative to total liabilities, because they lack the balance-sheet slack to absorb a shortfall in the new assets' payoff.
considered.reasoning: The investment leg broadens from capex alone to the full cash outlay on growth (with unreported acquisitions correctly read as zero), while the quality leg switches from cash-flow generation to a stock measure of balance-sheet slack, a dimension absent from the archive. This tests whether the funding-fragility mechanism operates through solvency slack as well as through cash-flow coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Investing into falling capital productivity
considered.hypothesis: Adding capacity while the existing asset base is generating progressively less revenue per dollar of assets signals overcapacity and demand misjudgment, whereas heavy investment accompanied by rising asset turnover reflects capacity that is already being absorbed.
considered.reasoning: The quality gauge is capital productivity change rather than a profitability or accrual level, so the signal is not another q-theory profitability interaction, and the denominators (ppent for investment intensity, at for turnover) avoid the mechanical small-PPE artifact that a sale/ppe pairing would create. Utilization deterioration is observable before margins deteriorate, so it may lead the profitability-based versions in the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-buffer depletion during expansion
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1), MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))))
considered.hypothesis: Heavy investment financed by drawing down liquid reserves at firms that also generate weak operating cash flow is the most fragile form of expansion, since both the internal flow and the stock of internal funding are being exhausted simultaneously.
considered.reasoning: This separates the stock (change in cash holdings) from the flow (three-year cash ROA) dimension of internal funding and co-ranks them, rather than using the capx-minus-oancf gap, so it is not a rescaling of the archive's winner but a test of whether the liquidity buffer carries independent information. Both inputs are densely reported, so coverage should exceed the archive's funding-gap signals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Five-year capital build-up without profitability payoff
considered.hypothesis: Investment should eventually show up in operating cash generation; firms that have accumulated a large multi-year capital build-up with no improvement in cash profitability over the same horizon have demonstrably invested unproductively, and the market is slow to write that capital down.
considered.reasoning: Rather than re-running the one-year funding-gap winner with cosmetic changes, this switches the mechanism to realized payoff over a matched five-year horizon: the investment leg is cumulative capex intensity (a capital-vintage state, not a growth rate) and the quality leg is the trend in cash ROA over the same window, so the signal asks whether accumulated capital earned anything. The interaction is the whole content — heavy builders with improving cash profitability sit long, heavy builders with flat or falling cash profitability sit short — which is distinct from external-financing dependence.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Expansion with stretched asset lives
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(dp, LAG(ppegt, 1)), MA(RATIO(dp, LAG(ppegt, 1)), 3)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that expand while recognizing less depreciation per dollar of beginning-of-year gross property than their own recent norm are stretching asset lives to support reported earnings, so their capital spending coincides with deteriorating accounting quality rather than genuine productivity.
considered.reasoning: The mechanical contamination is removed by measuring the depreciation rate against beginning-of-year gross PP&E, so assets purchased during the year do not inflate the denominator while contributing only partial-year depreciation, and by benchmarking against the firm's own three-year rate rather than the cross-section, which strips industry asset mix. What remains is policy drift in write-off intensity, interacted with capex intensity, giving a short leg of aggressive expanders with softening depreciation and a long leg of expanders who write off conservatively.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity added beyond internal funding capacity
considered.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is how far a firm's capacity additions exceed the cash its operations actually produced: large positive gaps are externally funded expansion, while large negative values are cash-generative firms holding capacity flat or shrinking, which should be rewarded.
considered.reasoning: Retaining the deficit magnitude on a common asset scale fixes the quadrant problem in the SIGN version: cash-rich firms that shrink now receive the most negative (bullish) values, consistent with both the asset-growth and profitability evidence, instead of being predicted to underperform. The construct is a single dense continuous variable with no rank attenuation, no zero mass, and both themes entering symmetrically, so a strong result is direct evidence that the investment-versus-internal-cash gap, not either level alone, is the priced quantity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Co-ranked outlay and solvency slack
considered.expression: SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), DELTA(invt, 1)), at), 1), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), lt), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Heavy total investment outlay combined with thin working-capital slack relative to liabilities identifies fragile expansion, and this relation should be monotone across the cross-section rather than confined to the extreme tails.
considered.reasoning: The multiplicative version delivered a −4.0 t-stat alpha but a null Fama-MacBeth slope, the signature of a product whose raw scale is dominated by a few extreme observations; replacing MUL with a bounded co-rank keeps the same two economic legs while making the signal monotone and outlier-insensitive, which should convert the portfolio spread into cross-sectional slope evidence as well. This isolates operator structure only, so the comparison is directly attributable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex intensity with weak debt-service capacity
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), ADD(dltt, dlc)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Capital spending is dangerous when cash earnings cover only a small fraction of outstanding debt, because the firm must keep servicing fixed claims while the new assets are still unproductive, forcing asset sales or dilution exactly when the investment fails to pay off.
considered.reasoning: Debt-service capacity (funds from operations over total debt) is a distinct fragility dimension from the flow funding gap, the cash buffer, or working-capital slack already tested, and it directly captures the claim-priority mechanism behind low-quality expansion. Funds from operations and debt balances are densely reported, so coverage should be at the higher end of the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex into a multi-year gross-profitability decline
considered.hypothesis: Adding capacity while gross profitability on the asset base has been declining for several years signals structural erosion of the business rather than a temporary dip, and such investment should be punished more than investment during a one-year turnover wobble.
considered.reasoning: The archive's capital-productivity signal produced a solid FMB slope but almost no alpha, consistent with a noisy one-year change in asset turnover producing unstable portfolio extremes; replacing it with a five-year trend in gross profit over assets smooths the quality leg and shifts the concept from utilization wobble to structural erosion. This isolates the smoothing/horizon choice while keeping the same capital-productivity mechanism.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Maturity-mismatched capital spending
considered.hypothesis: Long-lived physical investment financed against a liability structure concentrated in current obligations creates rollover risk during the gestation period before the assets produce cash, so heavy capex at firms whose liabilities are predominantly short-term should predict low returns even when the funding level looks adequate.
considered.reasoning: The quality dimension is liability *duration* rather than the level of internal funds, solvency slack, or cash buffer already tested, so this is new economic content: it says the mismatch between asset life and claim maturity — not the size of the funding gap — is what makes expansion fragile. The signed industry-standardized short-maturity share reorders capex intensity so that heavy investors funded with long-duration claims sit long, giving a genuine conditional interaction rather than an averaging of archive legs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Escalating capex despite poor marginal payoff
considered.hypothesis: The realized cash payoff on last year's capital spending is the market's best evidence on whether a firm's investment is productive; firms that keep spending heavily after their prior capital delivered little or no incremental operating cash flow are escalating commitment to failing projects.
considered.reasoning: This replaces an average-profitability or uncertainty gauge with a *marginal* return-on-new-capital measure — the change in operating cash flow per dollar of prior-year capex — which is a mechanism no archive signal and no standard investment anomaly captures. The interaction is essential: a low marginal payoff is only bearish for firms that are still spending, while high marginal payoff plus heavy spending identifies genuinely productive investment on the long side.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Aging capital base with weak cash generation
considered.hypothesis: A heavily depreciated capital stock means the productive base is old and due for replacement; firms in that state with weak cash generation cannot fund renewal and face obsolescence, whereas cash-rich firms with old assets can harvest or reinvest at will.
considered.reasoning: Capital vintage — accumulated depreciation as a share of gross property — is an investment-theme state variable measuring past *under*-investment, the opposite pole from every expansion measure in the archive, so this tests whether the theme interaction is symmetric or specific to overexpansion. Pairing it with three-year cash ROA distinguishes obsolescence traps (short leg) from mature cash-generative harvesters (long leg), and both inputs are densely reported.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Expansion financed through losses
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ib, at), ABS(RATIO(ib, at))), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Quality matters asymmetrically for investment: variation in profitability among already-profitable firms says little about whether capex is productive, but the depth of current losses says a great deal, because loss-making expanders must fund both operations and growth from outside capital.
considered.reasoning: The term ib/at minus its absolute value equals twice the loss magnitude and is exactly zero for every profitable firm, so the quality leg conditions only within the loss region instead of spreading weight across the whole profitability distribution — an asymmetric conditioning design the archive has never tested. The short leg is deep-loss heavy investors, the long leg is profitable heavy investors, which is precisely the productive-versus-fragile expansion contrast the theme asks for.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity growth with chronic deficit years
considered.hypothesis: What distinguishes structurally external-finance-dependent expanders from firms in a lumpy capex year is the *number* of past years in which investment exceeded operating cash flow; capacity growth by firms with a persistent deficit history should be the most value-destroying.
considered.reasoning: Counting deficit years over five years converts the funding-gap concept from a heavy-tailed magnitude into a bounded 0–5 state variable, so it cannot be dominated by outliers and it measures persistence rather than the current-year level — a different economic claim (chronic dependence) from the archive's one-year gap. If it beats the one-year winner on the FMB slope while holding the alpha, it identifies persistence as the operative fragility mechanism.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex with near-term refinancing pressure
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(capx, at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dlc, ADD(ib, dp)), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms committing cash to long-lived assets while their debt maturing within the year exceeds a full year of cash earnings face rollover risk exactly during the project gestation period, forcing distressed refinancing, asset sales, or dilution.
considered.reasoning: This repairs the failed maturity-mismatch signal, whose lct/lt leg inadvertently proxied for *low* leverage (giving the wrong sign); the replacement measures near-term debt net of annual funds from operations on a common asset scale, so loss-making firms with maturing debt score most fragile instead of being mis-ranked by a negative denominator. It is distinct from the FFO-to-total-debt signal because it isolates *timing* of claims rather than total leverage capacity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Inventory bloat with signed cash profitability
considered.hypothesis: Working-capital investment outrunning sales is bearish at cash-poor firms and largely innocuous at cash-generative firms, which can carry and eventually clear the inventory; the quality leg should therefore reorder the wedge rather than merely shrink it.
considered.reasoning: The gen-0 inventory-bloat winner used a non-negative ROA rank that could only attenuate, which the critic identified as its central weakness; replacing it with a signed, industry-standardized three-year cash-ROA and ranking the wedge itself makes high-bloat cash-poor firms the short leg and high-bloat cash-rich firms the long leg. This is an attributable single-element upgrade of an established archive winner along the dimension the critic flagged.
